zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical checkpoint after independent scan reading: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. Supplied page subset used for headword coverage only; diplomatic readings and commentary are this review's own. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

runs.text: porta aquem primeiro chegaria, eſperauão que

lines.note: Continues the preceding entry: waiting at the door for whoever would arrive first. The conditional chegaria and the plural eſperauão belong to this unfinished Portuguese sentence, not to a new entry.
Chegaßem completes the preceding expectation of arrival; the abbreviation &c. closes the carried-over explanation.
Machikooji denotes streets and side streets, matching ruas and traueßas. The enlarged accent is a circumflex, so Machicôgi replaces the provisional caron spelling.
Machigao is the expectant expression of someone waiting. Sembrante describes the face or expression, not a town-related sense of machi.
Machijin and Machǔdo are alternative names for a townsman. The printed l. introduces the alternative; the gloss continues with a resident of a settlement.
Morador de pouoação completes the definition of the town-dweller. The historical u/v spelling in pouoação is retained.
Machimachi means diverse or differing. Enlargement establishes the missing i in differente; the two f types remain distinct from the long s in diuerſa.

The example illustrates people expressing differing opinions, as the next row explains. Qigui is retained as printed rather than altered to a more familiar Japanese form; machimachini modifies yǔ. The final ca- begins Portuguese cada.
Da joins ca- above to form cada: each person states a different opinion. This closes the machimachi example.

runs.text: Couſa que ſe vende na rua, ou

lines.note: Machimono is merchandise sold in the street or a shop. The visible word gap gives na rua, not the OCR joining narua.

runs.text: tenda. ¶ Item, Couſa de fancaria, ou de

lines.note: Tenda completes the place of sale. The additional fancaria sense concerns ordinary stock or ready-made work and continues with corja on the next row.
The stock-made sense is explicitly contrasted with Atçurayemono, something made to order. This Japanese term is embedded in Portuguese explanatory prose and remains upright.
Machimǒqe, with the principal forms uru and eta, means obtaining or receiving something after waiting. The caron is visible here and is not assimilated to the different accent in Machicôgi.
The example begins receiving an expected guest: Qiacujinuo is the object, and machimǒqe continues with ta below. No terminal hyphen is supplied where none is visible.
Ta completes the past-tense example. Recebi hum hoſpede que eſperaua gives its first-person sense: receiving the guest one had been expecting.
Machitçucuxi means waiting exhaustively or for a long time. The printed principal part uita is a historical inflection, not an error to be modernized to ushita.

Cocorouo tçucuite describes applying oneself wholeheartedly; together with the following row it illustrates prolonged, careful waiting. Tçucuite has the same historical i-onbin pattern as the entry forms.

Sujit specifies several days, and machitçucuita completes the past-tense example. Tog. is an upright citation label. The Portuguese begins Cõ todo cui-, with a visible gap after Cõ and cuidado divided across the line.
Dado completes cuidado: the speaker waited many days with every care. The first-person eſtiue confirms that this is the translation of the preceding example.
Machitçuqe means waiting for someone until that person arrives. The infinitive explanation is completed by chegar on the next physical row.
Pedrouo machitçuqeta illustrates waiting until Pedro arrived. The complete name and attached Japanese object particle belong to the upright example, not partly to the italic Portuguese apparatus.
Machitçure describes waiting for someone and then taking that person along. The visibly printed ruru is preserved, rather than standardized to the more usual abbreviated uru.
Conſigo completes leuar: taking the awaited person with oneself. This short line is genuine continuation text.
Machitotonoye concerns preparing things while awaiting someone. Enlargement supports eta, not OCR cta; apa- begins Portuguese aparelhar on the next row.

runs.text: relhar, como quem vai concertando comer, &

lines.note: Relhar completes aparelhar. The gloss compares this preparation with arranging food while expecting a guest; concertando is retained in its historical sense of putting things in order.

runs.text: o de mais para conuidar a alguem.

lines.note: The preparation includes everything else needed to entertain someone. The spaced de mais is preserved rather than modernized to demais.
Machitto is an adverb meaning a little more. Adu. is italic grammatical apparatus, not part of the Japanese headword.
Machivqe means waiting to receive someone. The initial v of the second element represents the historical spelling of uke; al- divides Portuguese alguem.
The quoted example begins with confined places at various locations. No full stop is established after Xoxono; removing the OCR stop restores the visible continuous Japanese phrase.

Machi vqete vchitomeqeru describes waiting in ambush and striking someone down; aida continues the cited narrative construction. The printed internal gap in machi vqete is retained, and &c. is the closing apparatus.
Taif. is the upright source label, followed by italic Lib. 7. The Portuguese translation begins waiting for him in narrow places; eſtre- continues as eſtreitos below.

runs.text: itos, & apertados o matou, ou fez ficar morto.

lines.note: Itos completes eſtreitos. The rest explains killing him, or making him remain dead, in those restricted places; it closes the ambush example.
Machiya is simply glossed as houses in the street. The definition supports the town-house sense without adding a modern architectural classification.
Machiye is obtaining something after waiting. The following wind example distinguishes this verb from the preceding noun Machiya.
Sono cajeuo machiyete describes obtaining the awaited wind. The damaged a in cajeuo is compatible with the remaining strokes and the Portuguese vento; the historical caje spelling is not normalized.
Que eſperaua completes the wind example: the wind that the person had been waiting for. The short line remains separate body text.

runs.text: Homem da rua, ou morador de

lines.note: Machǔdo repeats the townsman term already offered as an alternative under Machijin. The gloss again defines a resident, rather than a person who is waiting.
Villa or cidade supplies the settlement in which the townsman lives. Both alternatives complete morador de on the preceding row.

Macocoro is explained as a true heart, with magocoro as an alternative. Enlargement supports damaged cocoro: the apparent cedilla in the OCR crosses a paper crease and is not a secure printed mark. This local reading remains mildly uncertain because the first two letters are abraded.
The Portuguese gives a true and straightforward heart. The paragraph mark then introduces the horse example, whose Macocorona is divided after Ma-.
Macocorona vma describes a gentle, well-disposed horse. The scan supports manſo instead of OCR iranſo; bo- begins boas on the following row.
As completes boas: the horse has good habits or qualities. It belongs to the horse example, not to the following plant entry.

runs.text: Hũa certa erua de agua doce como

lines.note: Macomo is described as a freshwater plant resembling a rush. The readable phrase erua de agua doce corrects the garbled OCR; no precise botanical identification is imported into the text.
Bunho completes the comparison with a rush. This one-word botanical continuation is not a new headword.
Macomo. Muxiro names a mat made from the preceding plant. Both printed stops and the capital Muxiro are preserved; enlargement supports the t in deſta, rather than OCR deſa.
Macoto is truth, directly matched by Verdade. The spelling is kept distinct from the following adverbial form.
Macotoni means truly or certainly. The damaged initial is M, not the OCR sequence Du, and the Portuguese reads certamente, not centamente.
Macotono is the attributive expression for something true. The scan has an initial M, continuing the macoto family, rather than OCR Nacotono.
Macotoraxij describes something that appears true. The gloss concerns the appearance of truth, not necessarily its actuality.
Macotoxij receives Idem, explicitly referring back to the preceding appearance-of-truth definition.
Macotoxiyacani is an adverb meaning as though something were true. The final ni and the italic label Adu. identify its adverbial use.
Macoto xiyacani tabacaru means deceiving in a plausible or truth-like manner. The printed gap within Macoto xiyacani is preserved even though the headword is unspaced.

runs.text: a alguẽ fazendo o crir mentira por verdade.

lines.note: The Portuguese explains making someone believe a lie as truth. The visibly printed crir is retained rather than normalized to crer, and alguẽ keeps its abbreviation tilde.

runs.text: Cortinas compridas que ſeruem nas em-

lines.note: Macu denotes long curtains or screens. The explanation begins listing their uses, with em- continuing as embarcações.
The curtains are used on vessels, with armies, and in performances. Autos is theatrical here; Ma- begins the first curtain-setting example.
Macuuo faru means extending or putting up curtains in theatres. The initial cuuo completes Ma- from the preceding row.
Macuuo faxiracaſu is the expression for setting curtains on a ship. Por is the historical infinitive meaning put, not the Portuguese preposition in this construction.

The shipboard explanation ends before the next example, whose vtçu is divided between this row and the next. A separate second-pass enlargement shows a round point after v, not a secure hyphen; the original v. is therefore retained despite the continuation.
Tçu completes vtçu, the verb used for erecting the screens in an army setting. Eſtendelas refers back to the curtains.

runs.text: Coua do olho muito metido pera

lines.note: Macubo denotes a deeply hollowed eye socket. The Portuguese locates the eye as very far inward, with the direction completed below.
Dentro completes pera dentro. The final B. is an upright low-register label, distinct from the italic gloss.
Macubari means distributing in proportion. The abbreviated principal forms u and atta are retained exactly as printed, without silently supplying r.
Ninjuuo macubari auaſuru describes distributing people in balanced proportions. Repar- begins the Portuguese restatement on the next row.

runs.text: tir a gente de maneira que fiquem igualmente

lines.note: Tir completes repartir. The distribution is arranged so that the people are placed equally, with the participial phrase continuing below.
The people are assigned to their respective stations. Faxirauo begins a second example, this time about the spacing of pillars rather than personnel.
Faxirauo macubaru means distributing the pillars at appropriate intervals. The Portuguese columnas confirms the architectural object.
Eſpaços completes the allocation of the columns to their spaces or intervals. It is an ordinary continuation, not a heading.
Macuguxi and macuzucuxi name the stakes or poles that support military curtains. The alternative marker l remains literal, and pa- continues as paos.

runs.text: os de que ſe dependurão as cortinas no exercito.

lines.note: Os completes paos. These are the poles from which the curtains are suspended in an army setting; the historical dependurão is retained.
Macujen is explained as a manner of remaining quiet and inactive. The crop clearly reads Modo, not OCR Medo; this is not a definition involving fear.
Macujento xite iru illustrates staying quietly without doing anything. The abbreviated ſẽ belongs to the Portuguese explanation, while the Japanese example remains upright.

Macumǒjǒ is paraphrased as being quiet and thinking idly or without discipline. The following Portuguese gloss characterizes the thoughts negatively; the historical Xizzucanari is retained without syntactic modernization.
The synonym mǒnen reinforces the sense of idle or misguided thoughts. Ruins penſamentos begins the Portuguese definition, followed by divided conſi-deração.
Deração completes conſideração: reflection on vain things. This closes the thought-related entry before Macura begins the pillow vocabulary.
Macura means a pillow or headrest. The gloss reads Almofada, with f rather than the OCR long s; Macurauo cata- begins the first example.
Muquru completes catamuquru. The dictionary explains the expression as arranging the pillow for sleep, a contextual gloss retained rather than replaced by a literal modern translation.
Macurauo naraburu is placing pillows side by side. The Portuguese explanation begins arranging the pillow and continues with the purpose below.
Fada completes almofada: the arrangement is for two people to sleep together. The continuation supplies the point of the preceding Japanese example.

runs.text: Almofada de pao com algũs bu-

lines.note: Macurabaco is first described as a wooden headrest with openings. The line ends algũs bu-, not the joined OCR algũsba-; bu- continues as buracos on the next row.

runs.text: racos, ou aberturas polas quaes as molheres ſe

lines.note: Racos completes buracos. The holes or openings allow women to perfume themselves, with the action and means continued on the next row.

runs.text: perfumão com cheiro q̃ metẽ dentro. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Perfume placed inside the headrest provides the scent. The final e of metẽ carries a visible abbreviation tilde; the OCR omitted it. Itẽ introduces a second sense.

runs.text: Aliquando, Caixa em que metem a almofada.

lines.note: Aliquando marks the occasional sense: a box into which the pillow is put. This is distinguished from the perforated wooden headrest just described.

Macurabeǒbu denotes small, low screens beside the pillow. The Portuguese plural reads Beòbus, with a grave over o, not OCR Bedbus; the different caron in the upright headword is preserved independently.

Macuracotoba introduces poetic expressions, described here as words like synonyms. This is the dictionary's explanation of their poetic function, not a reason to replace it with a modern technical definition.

runs.text: vſão os poetas com artificio do verſo como pera

lines.note: The poets use such expressions as a device of verse. The line leads into two examples, beginning with the expression associated with earth.
Aracane is the example connected with terra. Enlargement establishes the arch of n rather than OCR u in Aracaue; the term occurs within Portuguese explanation and remains upright.
Tamaboco supplies the example associated with a road. The final &c. is upright here, unlike the italic Portuguese connective opening the row.
Macuragami is the head of the bed. Ma- begins the example of standing at the sleeping person's bedside.
Macuragamini tatçu means standing at the head of the bed. Portuguese Porſe em pè expresses taking up a standing position; cabecei- continues below.
Ra completes cabeceira, specified as that of the person sleeping. It closes the position example.

runs.text: Hũa lança curta que ſe poem pe-

lines.note: Macurayari is a short spear kept beside the pillow. The headword has y, not OCR j; the description continues after pe-.
Ra completes pera: the spear is kept for watch or protection at the head of the bed. The crop reads cabeceira, not the OCR cabeceita.
Macuri means uncovering by rolling up or gathering a covering. The full Portuguese verb is Deſcobrir, rather than the truncated OCR Deſchrir; the printed principal part u remains unexpanded.

The covering is gathered up. Yaneuo macuru introduces removing a roof covering, whose Portuguese explanation starts on f301; the printed closing mark after macuru is a comma. The lower isolated deſtelhar is a catchword, not a second body continuation.
